journal.hardwrought.down_through_the_roc: A mine runs out one day; the rock under it never does. A drill head, driven from below and set in a frame of metal, works its way through the whole ground under a chunk. Every chunk holds its own mix of ores, and how deep the drill reaches is decided by the weakest metal in its frame: bronze brings up coal and iron, titanium everything.
journal.hardwrought.moving_it_along.text: A drill that has to be emptied by hand is only half a machine. A pipe of plate metal, laid from its chute, takes the ore wherever the pipe goes and puts it into the nearest chest or furnace with room for it. The metal decides the pace: bronze carries one piece a second, iron eight, nickel twenty, chromium eighty, titanium more than anything can fill it with.

journal.hardwrought.a_bath_of_metal.text: A forge brings metal to working heat and never further. To make it run, the fire has to be shut in: a floor and walls of refractory brick around an empty space, one block in the wall to tend it and one to let the metal out. Coal alone melts only the soft metals; iron wants air blown in, or coal burnt to coke first. What runs from the drain wants a mould of fired clay to set in.
journal.hardwrought.harder_than_iron.tex: Iron takes an edge, but does not keep it. Molten iron that has taken up coal in the bath comes out harder: four parts iron to one of carbon, and coal ground to powder gives the carbon. The bath has to be hotter than iron melts before the two will join. Cast into bars, it forges like iron, only better. Left wet, though, it rusts.
journal.hardwrought.black_gold.title: Black Gold
journal.hardwrought.black_gold.text: The layered rock that was once the floor of a sea smells of tar in places. Something that burns must lie under it, held in by a tight layer. A shaft turned by water or wind could bore a pipe down to it. But careful: what comes up first is gas, and gas with no way out waits for the first flame. The oil itself is good for nothing until it is parted over a fire.

journal.hardwrought.first_edge.title: Something with an edge
journal.hardwrought.first_edge.text: My hands do nothing against rock or standing timber. I have to put an edge between them and me, and it has to be harder than both. There is a dark, glassy stone in the gravel and along the riverbeds that does not crumble — it splits, and where it splits it is sharper than anything else I have picked up. Tying one to a handle is the other half of the problem: leaves stripped off by hand give up a fibre that holds.
journal.hardwrought.bench_from_the_trunk: A bench out of the trunk

Two squares by two in my hands is not room enough for real work, and I have no way to saw a board. But a hatchet and a standing trunk might be. Felling it is not the point — the tree can stay where it is. Crouch against it, keep working the same spot, and do not stop after the first few strokes: it takes far more of them than it feels like it should.
journal.hardwrought.firmer_than_flint.te: Flint takes an edge and loses it again just as fast; a few good blows and the head is ruined. Now that I can break rock at all, the tougher material is in my own hands. A whole block of it is far too coarse to bind to a handle — but it comes apart into smaller pieces, and a head made of those lasts.
journal.hardwrought.heat_that_holds.text: An open fire cooks meat, and with a great deal of patience it will bake wet clay hard. That is as far as it goes; the heat goes straight up and is gone. What I need is something that keeps it in. The baked clay itself is the material for that — hard, all of a size, and it stacks. Enough of it, set into a closed square, and I have an oven instead of a fire pit.
journal.hardwrought.at_the_anvil.title: Iron wants hammering
journal.hardwrought.at_the_anvil.text: The rusty lumps come out of the oven as rusty lumps, only hotter. Heat alone does not make metal of them; the rock has to be beaten out of it while it glows, and beaten into a bar. That wants three things I do not have. Something to strike on that gives a little and does not split — the end grain of a thick trunk, not stone. Something heavier than my fist to strike with. And hands that can hold a glowing lump without being burnt to the bone: leather, thick, sewn to fit.
journal.hardwrought.rust_in_the_rock.tex: A bar of iron is not yet a tool. A head has to be drawn out of it at the anvil, shaped while it is hot, blow by blow — and a bad blow shows in the finished edge for ever. Several bars for a pick head, one will do for a shovel. Once the head has cooled, a handle through it, and it is a tool that holds an edge my stone hatchet is a toy beside.
journal.hardwrought.fire_and_water.title: Fire and water
journal.hardwrought.fire_and_water.text: A head that cools in the air is tough and soft. Plunged into water while it still glows, iron comes out hard — hard enough to take a real edge, and brittle with it. Warmed again, gently, only just too hot to touch, it keeps most of the hardness and loses the brittleness. An oven cannot do gentle. A proper hearth can, and with air driven through it by leather and boards it gets hotter than any oven I have built. Lined with brick that does not crack in the fire, hotter still.
journal.hardwrought.breaking_it_finer.te: Lumps of ore do not mix; melted side by side they only sit next to each other. Whatever I want to blend has to be ground first, finer than a hammer and a flat stone will ever get it, and far more of it than my arms have patience for. Stone jaws in a wooden frame would do the grinding, if something kept them moving. A bar that turns will carry the turning from wherever I stand — and the simplest thing that turns a bar is a handle, and me on the end of it.
journal.hardwrought.two_soft_metals.text: Copper on its own bends under the work; it is too soft for a tool. But there is a second metal, rarer, and it is not cut out of a seam at all — it is washed out of river gravel, a little at a time. Ground to powder, the two will blend where lumps never would. Three parts of the first to one of the second is where I would start, and then back into the heat. Together they are not what either one is alone.
The bench I cut out of the trunk wobbles, and there is work it will not take: anything with metal in it wants a surface that stays put. It does not have to be built again from nothing. Bronze holds a point, and a handful of it drawn out thin would pin the top to what is left of the trunk — right where it stands. My fist will not drive them, though. A stone head on a stick will, one blow after another, for as long as it takes.

journal.hardwrought.something_to_carry.t: My hands and my belt hold nine things and not one more. Anything else I find, I have to leave where it lies. Leaves stripped by hand give a green fibre; it binds a tool as it is, but to twist it into cord it has to dry in the sun first, on a few sticks. Cord can be woven, if I had a needle — and a stick rubbed long enough on stone comes to a point. Four pieces of cloth sewn together would make something to carry on my back. It will take patience and more nights than I would like.
recipe.hardwrought.drying_fibre.instruct: Hang green fibre on a drying rack under open sky. It dries only in daylight and dry weather: half a day of sun.
journal.hardwrought.more_on_my_back.text: The woven pack sags as soon as it is full, and it carries a row of things at most. Lashed to a frame of sticks, with more cloth and cord, it would keep its shape and hold twice as much. A proper bench would make the lashing easier. After that, only leather will do.
